concept.name: Blockchain
concept.definition: A blockchain is a shared, append-only database maintained by many computers in a network, in which transaction data is grouped into blocks and each block cryptographically references its parent, so that altering past data requires redoing all subsequent blocks and network consensus.
concept.intuition: Think of it as a public ledger copied onto thousands of computers: everyone holds the same history, and no single party can quietly rewrite it.
concept.mechanics: Transactions are batched into blocks; each block contains a hash of the previous block, chaining them together. Nodes independently verify every new block against consensus rules, and a consensus mechanism (e.g. proof-of-work or proof-of-stake) decides which blocks extend the canonical chain.
concept.failure_modes: A 51% attack or consensus failure can reorganize recent blocks, reversing transactions; software bugs in dominant client implementations can halt or split the chain.
concept.misconceptions: Blockchains are not inherently immutable at the tip — recent blocks can be reorganized, which is why confirmations or finality matter. Not every blockchain is decentralized or permissionless; private chains exist.
concept.example: If you send ETH to someone, the transaction is included in a block; on proof-of-stake Ethereum, after roughly two epochs (~13 minutes) the block containing it is finalized and cannot be reverted without at least one-third of staked ETH being destroyed.

citations.source: Ethereum.org developer docs - Introduction to Ethereum
